1. What will the weather be like tomorrow?

  • Announcer: Here is the weather forecast. Today will be very cloudy, although it won’t rain until the evening. The weather tomorrow will be the same as yesterday – sunshine and showers. But the weekend looks good – plenty of sunshine and very little rain.

2. What will the man do first?

  • Woman: Steve, what are you going to do today?
  • Man: Mmm ... well, I’ve got to have my hair cut, but before I do anything I need to ring Peter and see if he wants to play golf.
  • Woman: That’s a good idea, you haven’t played for a while, have you?

3. Where is the knife?

  • Woman: I’m glad we decided to stop here for our picnic. Can you find the knife for me, and I’ll cut up the cucumber? I packed it in the bag with the bread ... oh, but I used it to peel some oranges when we stopped in the petrol station so it’ll be with them. I hope it’s big enough to cut up this pie.

4. What happened to the girl this afternoon?

  • Girl: You’ll never guess what happened to me this afternoon! I was cycling over the bridge in town, when there was this really strong wind, and I fell off my bike. I didn’t hurt myself, but my books were thrown onto the pavement and went everywhere. This really nice boy picked them up for me! It’s lucky there were no cars around to drive over my bike, which was still in the road. I thanked the boy, then I picked up my bike and cycled away. I was ...

5. Which man is waiting at the bus stop?

  • Boy: Oh look, that’s my new English teacher over there, see – he’s waiting at the bus stop.
  • Girl: The young one with sunglasses and blond hair? You always told me your teacher was bald and really old and got angry because he kept losing his glasses.
  • Boy: That was the teacher I had before. This one is really nice.

6. What time does the television programme end?

  • Mum: Go to bed, Luke. It’s already twenty to eleven and you’ve got to be up early in the morning.
  • Boy: Aw, mum, just another few minutes. I’m watching this brilliant TV programme about American football. It’ll be over at 10 to and I can be in bed by 10 past. Nobody in my class has to go to bed before 11 o’clock. It’s not fair.

7. Which postcard will they send to Mark?

  • Man: I’m getting this postcard of that bridge in the old city for my parents. And this church looks nice – shall we send it to Mark? He likes old buildings.
  • Woman: But we haven’t actually been there – we should send him a card of something we’ve actually seen. Here’s the beach we went to yesterday.
  • Man: But it looks horrible and crowded in that picture.
  • Woman: Oh, just get him the same one as you’re sending to your parents.

8. Which present will the girl take?

  • Girl: I really don’t know what to give Mrs Allemano when I go and stay with her in New York. Do you think she’d like some perfume?
  • Man: Well, you don’t know her very well, do you, so I’d choose something like a scarf, or just a box of chocolates.
  • Girl: Umm ... I like your first idea best – it’ll be much easier to carry.

  • Man: Right. I see both here but Lisa is the one I want for ID purposes (4). And your date of birth, Lisa? ... I mean Marie.

  • Woman: Good morning, Travel Link. How can I help you?
  • Man: Good morning. I live in Bayswater and I’d like to get to Harbour City tomorrow (1) before 11.am.
  • Woman: Well, to get to Bayswater....
  • Man: No, no. I live in Bayswater – my destination is Harbour City (1).

  • Man: I don’t mind really. Whichever option is faster, I suppose.

  • Man: Did you say Helensvale?

  • Man: What’s the best way to get to the Helendale station then?

  • Elena: She’s artistic and doesn’t really care what people think or say about her, or get upset about how people behave. I’m a lot like that too (Q1). I don’t worry too much about other people's opinions of me.
  • Interviewer: So is being free of worry a message you wanted to communicate to your audience?
  • Elena: In a way. You need to be free. You shouldn’t be tied to your background, where you were born or anything you haven't chosen for yourself. People have dreams and I guess I’m saying that (Q2) they should have belief in themselves, that they can make those dreams come real.
  • Interviewer: It must have been an exciting atmosphere to work in. Was making the film like your own dream coming true?
  • Elena: Definitely, although it wasn’t easy. (Q3) I had very little time or money. People told me to relax but I knew I couldn’t - if I didn’t work, no one else would! But after a week or so because everyone on the film was facing the same challenge we came together. When we all left at the end it was sad because it was like a family breaking up.
  • Interviewer: Tell me about a typical day's filming.
  • Elena: I don’t think there was a typical day really. Each day I got up at 5 to start at 6. (Q4) I’d film two or three scenes in the morning and the same again after lunch. That way I had a goal and I knew how much I was achieving each day. Sometimes, if we needed to we'd work on until late, till 3 a.m. one time! I really enjoyed my Sundays off!

tasks.tapescript:
Talk 1: Ecotourism

Ecotourism is a booming business that many tour operators cite as being helpful to nature. Every year, millions of people descend on protected and pristine natural areas to observe rare species. However, a new report casts doubt on the value of this form of tourism. In fact, it suggests that ecotourism is more damaging than helpful to nature. Details are in a report published in the journal 'Trends in Ecology and Evolution'. Researchers believe tourists are disrupting animals in their natural habitat. They pointed to a recent event where sea turtles in Costa Rica had problems laying their eggs because of the hordes of tourists who had congregated to watch the turtles' nesting habits.

The report says that ecotourism is making animals bolder and that this could endanger the animals. A regular human presence might make animals tamer and less cautious about other animals around them, and this could put them at risk of being attacked by their natural threats. "Then they will suffer higher mortality when they encounter real predators," the report says. It added: "When animals interact in 'benign' ways with humans, they may let down their guard." The report said it was essential, "to develop a more comprehensive understanding of how different species in different situations respond to human visitation and under what precise conditions human exposure might put them at risk."

Talk 2: Skin-lightening Creams

An association of local governments in the UK, called the LGA, has warned consumers about the use of some skin-lightening creams. The LGA discovered that some of the whitening cosmetics they tested contained banned ingredients and were thus illegal. However, they were available for purchase in UK stores. An LGA spokesperson said these ingredients could pose a serious threat to consumers' health. He said there has been an increase in the number of users experiencing health problems after using the creams. These include seizures, rashes and scarring. The spokesperson said the creams could increase the risk of skin cancer, and liver and kidney damage.

The global skin-lightening industry is booming. In 2017, it was valued at an estimated $4.8 billion and is forecast to nearly double to around $8.9 billion in the next decade. Many people use it to reduce the darkness of the color of their skin. The LGA warned that "rogue retailers" were selling illegal skin-lightening lotions on which the label incorrectly listed the ingredients and omitted the illegal substances. The LGA said some illegal ingredients acted like paint stripper and could burn off the top layer of skin. It said: "Skin creams containing banned ingredients are very dangerous and could seriously damage your health, scar you for life and even kill you, so they should be avoided at all costs."

Talk 3: Parental Happiness

Many of us believe that having children is the key to happiness and a perfect family life. Naturally, this idealistic image is true for some, but researchers say that in reality, children make us happiest when they fly the nest - when they have grown up and left home. Researchers in Germany looked at data from a survey of 55,000 over 50-year-olds living in Europe. The survey respondents were quizzed about their emotional wellbeing. The researchers discovered that most parents were happier with life after their offspring had left home and started making their own way in life. Researchers say this could be because raising children creates financial worry, stress, fatigue and anxiety.

The research was led by Christoph Becker at Heidelberg University. He concluded that a big reason for parents being happiest when their children leave home is that the tables are turned and the children provide more support to their parents. He said parents whose children no longer live with them suffer from fewer symptoms of depression and have a more positive outlook on life. Regarding the role reversal in providing support, Mr Becker said: "Children's roles as caregivers, providers of financial support or simply as a means of social contact might outweigh the negative aspects of parenthood." He added that maintaining family relationships may stave off loneliness in ageing parents.

passage.title: The 'Kangaroo Family' in Korea
passage.text:
In South Korea, many families make a difficult choice so that their children can learn English well: the mother and children move to an English-speaking country such as the United States, Canada, or New Zealand, while the father stays behind in Korea to work and send money. This kind of family has come to be known informally as a 'kangaroo family,' since the children stay close to one parent, much like a baby kangaroo staying near its mother, while the other parent lives far away for years at a time. The arrangement usually begins when parents decide that early exposure to English will give their children a real advantage later in school and in their careers.

Life for the children in this arrangement often looks quite different from life back home. They attend local schools abroad, make new friends, and slowly become comfortable speaking English in daily conversations, something that can take years to achieve through classroom study alone. Meanwhile, the father who remains in Korea usually continues working long hours at his regular job, living alone in an apartment that once held the whole family. He might see his wife and children only once or twice a year, often during school holidays, when he saves vacation days and money for a short visit or when the family flies back to Korea.

This separation comes with a real burden that goes beyond money, even though the financial cost alone is already significant for most families. Supporting two households in two different countries, including rent, school fees, and travel expenses, can place enormous pressure on a single income. Fathers who live this way sometimes describe feeling lonely and disconnected from their children's daily lives, missing small moments such as a child's first day at a new school or a family dinner that happens without them.

Not everyone agrees that the kangaroo family lifestyle is worth these sacrifices. Critics argue that children can now learn English through many other methods, including online classes, video calls, and international schools inside Korea itself, without breaking up the family for years at a time. Supporters counter that living inside an English-speaking country still offers something video lessons cannot fully replace: constant, natural exposure to the language in everyday situations, from ordering food to making friends at school.

In recent years, the number of kangaroo families has slowly decreased, partly because international schools and online English programs inside Korea have improved so much that some parents no longer see the separation as necessary. Even so, for families who still believe strongly in the benefits of studying abroad, the kangaroo family remains a familiar, if difficult, path toward giving their children a stronger command of English.

passage.title: Individualism: A Useful but Imperfect Lens
passage.text:
Among the concepts that shape how psychologists and sociologists compare cultures across the globe, few have proven as influential, or as contested, as individualism — broadly defined as a cultural orientation that prioritizes personal autonomy, individual achievement, and self-expression over group harmony and collective obligation. Its conceptual counterpart, collectivism, emphasizes interdependence, family loyalty, and social duty instead, and the tension between these two orientations has become a foundational framework for understanding cross-cultural difference, even as scholars increasingly question how cleanly real societies map onto either category.

The modern popularity of this framework owes much to research conducted in the late twentieth century that ranked dozens of countries along an individualism-collectivism spectrum based on workplace attitudes and values surveys. Nations such as the United States, Australia, and much of Western Europe consistently scored toward the individualist end, while many East Asian, African, and Latin American societies scored closer to the collectivist end, a pattern that subsequent decades of research have largely, though not uniformly, replicated. Critics of this early work have since pointed out that the original data came almost entirely from employees of a single multinational corporation, raising legitimate questions about how representative those rankings ever truly were of entire national cultures.

In practical terms, individualist orientations tend to manifest in everyday decisions that many people in such societies barely notice as culturally shaped at all: choosing a career based primarily on personal interest rather than family expectation, moving away from one's hometown for education or work without this being considered unusual, or expecting children, once grown, to establish financially independent households of their own. Collectivist orientations, by contrast, more often involve extended family members participating directly in major life decisions, multigenerational households remaining the norm well into adulthood, and workplace loyalty being expressed through group harmony rather than individual recognition.

Whether entire nations can be meaningfully described as individualist or collectivist at all has become one of the framework's most persistent criticisms, and the skepticism is not without empirical grounding. Substantial variation exists within every country studied — urban and rural populations, different socioeconomic classes, and successive generations often diverge from a nation's supposed cultural average by margins large enough to make any single national score feel, to many researchers, like a statistical convenience rather than an accurate description of lived experience for most individuals within that country.

Research examining how individualism relates to psychological wellbeing has produced a genuinely mixed picture rather than a clear verdict in either direction. Some studies suggest that individualist values correlate with higher self-reported life satisfaction, possibly because personal autonomy allows people to pursue goals more closely aligned with their own preferences rather than externally imposed expectations. Other research, however, finds that strong social support networks, more characteristic of collectivist societies, may buffer against loneliness and certain forms of psychological distress more effectively than individual autonomy alone can, suggesting that neither orientation holds a straightforward wellbeing advantage over the other once other variables are properly accounted for.

Globalization has further complicated the individualism-collectivism distinction by exposing younger generations in traditionally collectivist societies to individualist media, education systems, and professional norms, often producing what researchers term 'hybrid' cultural identities that resist easy classification along a single spectrum. A young professional in Seoul or São Paulo might, for instance, hold strongly individualist career ambitions while simultaneously maintaining deeply collectivist obligations toward aging parents, illustrating that the two orientations may coexist within a single person rather than functioning as mutually exclusive cultural categories.

Despite its limitations, the individualism-collectivism framework has not been abandoned so much as refined, with contemporary researchers increasingly treating it as one useful lens among several rather than a complete explanation of cultural difference. Whether future cross-cultural psychology retains this framework in something close to its current form, or gradually replaces it with more granular models that better capture within-country variation, remains an open question that the field has not yet definitively resolved.

passage.title: Vietnam's Coffee Paradox
passage.text:
Vietnam's emergence as one of the world's leading coffee producers represents something of a paradox: a country with a coffee-growing history spanning barely a century and a half has, within the past three decades, come to rival nations with far older cultivation traditions in terms of sheer export volume. This rapid ascent, driven less by inherited expertise than by a combination of favorable geography, government policy, and sheer scale of production, has reshaped global coffee markets in ways that few observers anticipated when Vietnam's modern coffee sector began taking shape in the 1980s.

Coffee cultivation arrived in Vietnam under French colonial administration in the late nineteenth century, initially as a plantation crop intended primarily for export back to France rather than for domestic consumption. Unlike many coffee-growing regions that favored the more delicate arabica variety, Vietnam's climate and soil, particularly in the Central Highlands, proved especially well suited to robusta, a hardier species that yields a stronger, more bitter brew and tolerates heat and pest pressure considerably better than its more temperamental cousin. This early agronomic choice, made largely for practical rather than flavor-driven reasons, would go on to define the country's coffee identity for well over a century.

The vast majority of Vietnam's coffee is grown not on large industrial plantations but on smallholder farms, often just one or two hectares in size, cultivated by families who frequently depend on coffee for the greater share of their household income. This fragmented structure brings clear advantages, including flexibility and resilience against the kind of large-scale crop failure that can devastate a single massive plantation, yet it also leaves individual farmers with comparatively little bargaining power against the intermediaries and exporters who ultimately determine the prices those farmers receive for their harvest.

Vietnamese coffee farmers remain acutely exposed to price volatility that originates almost entirely outside their control, and this vulnerability is not merely an occasional inconvenience but a structural feature of how the global coffee trade operates. International robusta prices, set primarily on commodity exchanges in London and elsewhere, can swing significantly within a single growing season due to factors ranging from weather events in competing producer countries to shifts in currency exchange rates, leaving even well-managed smallholder farms financially exposed regardless of the quality or volume of coffee they manage to produce.

While the vast majority of Vietnamese coffee has historically been grown for export, domestic consumption has grown substantially in recent decades, giving rise to a distinctive café culture that blends traditional and contemporary elements. Cà phê sữa đá, strong drip coffee served over ice with sweetened condensed milk, remains the most iconic preparation, though newer inventions such as egg coffee, in which whipped egg yolk creates a custard-like foam atop the drink, have attracted considerable attention from younger consumers and international visitors alike, alongside a growing specialty coffee movement that increasingly champions higher-grade arabica alongside traditional robusta.

Climate change poses a threat to Vietnamese coffee production that researchers describe as considerably more serious than most farmers currently appreciate, since robusta, despite its relative hardiness compared to arabica, still requires fairly specific temperature and rainfall patterns to produce consistent yields. Rising temperatures and increasingly erratic rainfall across the Central Highlands have already begun reducing yields in some districts, while excessive groundwater extraction for irrigation, a practice many farmers adopted precisely because rainfall has grown less predictable, has itself begun to lower water tables in ways that may eventually threaten the long-term viability of coffee farming in certain areas.

Taken together, Vietnam's coffee industry illustrates how a genuine export success story can coexist with structural vulnerabilities that remain largely unresolved. Whether smallholder farmers can be better protected against price volatility, whether climate adaptation measures can be scaled quickly enough to matter, and whether the country's growing domestic coffee culture can meaningfully diversify an economy still heavily dependent on a single commodity crop are questions that will likely determine the industry's trajectory considerably more than its impressive export statistics alone.

passage.title: The Elusive Bangkok-Singapore Rail Corridor
passage.text:
The idea of a continuous rail line linking Bangkok to Singapore has circulated among planners and politicians for well over a century, surviving colonial administrations, world wars, and countless changes of government without ever being fully realized in the form early proponents imagined. What exists today across Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore is less a unified corridor than a patchwork of separately developed networks, some dating to early twentieth-century colonial construction and others reflecting far more recent, and considerably more ambitious, engineering efforts.

Much of the existing track across Malaysia and southern Thailand still runs on meter-gauge rail, a narrower standard than the 1,435-millimeter 'standard gauge' used in most of the world's newer high-speed systems, a legacy of decisions made by British colonial administrators more concerned with construction cost than with long-term interoperability. This gauge mismatch, seemingly a minor technical detail, has proven remarkably consequential: trains built for one gauge cannot simply run on the other, meaning any future seamless connection would likely require either extensive new standard-gauge construction or costly conversion of existing meter-gauge lines, neither of which any government has yet fully committed to funding.

The proposed high-speed rail link between Kuala Lumpur and Singapore illustrates just how difficult regional rail cooperation has proven even between two relatively wealthy, geographically adjacent nations. First formally proposed in the early 2010s and intended to cut journey times between the two capitals to roughly ninety minutes, the project has been suspended, revived, renegotiated, and suspended again multiple times, with disagreements over cost-sharing, technology providers, and station locations repeatedly derailing timelines that officials on both sides had, at various points, described with considerable confidence as final.

Thailand's own standard-gauge ambitions have centered on a Chinese-backed line intended eventually to connect Bangkok with Kunming via Laos, a project whose economic and strategic significance, however contested the details of its financing have proven, is difficult to dismiss entirely. Construction has proceeded in phases rather than as a single continuous build, with early sections opening years behind initial projections, and questions about technology transfer, debt financing terms, and the eventual division of operating revenue between Thai and Chinese entities remain, according to officials close to the negotiations, only partially resolved even as track-laying continues.

Coordinating rail infrastructure across three sovereign nations, each with its own funding priorities, regulatory frameworks, and domestic political pressures, has proven considerably harder in practice than the relatively straightforward engineering challenge might suggest on paper. Singapore, with its comparatively small domestic rail network and correspondingly limited direct stake in cross-border freight, has historically approached joint projects somewhat more cautiously than Malaysia or Thailand, both of which stand to gain more directly from expanded regional freight capacity, a divergence in incentive that has repeatedly complicated efforts to align the three countries around a single technical standard or shared timeline.

Proponents of a fully connected Bangkok-Singapore corridor point to substantial potential gains in tourism revenue and freight efficiency, arguing that a seamless standard-gauge link could shift meaningful volumes of cargo away from congested road networks and toward considerably more energy-efficient rail transport. Skeptics counter that the economic case, while plausible in broad outline, rests on freight and passenger volume projections that have not yet been rigorously tested against the region's actual trade patterns, and that similar infrastructure projects elsewhere have sometimes underperformed initial ridership and freight forecasts by considerable margins once actually operational.

Whether a genuinely continuous, standard-gauge rail corridor from Bangkok to Singapore ultimately materializes within the coming decade, or instead remains, as it has for much of the past century, a recurring proposal perpetually deferred by shifting political and financial circumstances, will likely depend less on any single breakthrough than on the simultaneous alignment of financing, political will, and technical standardization across all three governments — a combination that, based on the project's history to date, has proven considerably harder to achieve than any individual component of it.

Tiếp đó, thực hiện đọc quét dữ kiện cho các câu Chi tiết (R4Q2, R4Q4, R4Q8) và câu Loại trừ (R4Q6). Sau cùng, dựa trên bức tranh thông tin toàn cảnh đã ráp nối, bạn sẽ dễ dàng lựa chọn phương án chính xác cho các câu đòi hỏi tư duy tổng hợp gồm Suy luận (R4Q7), Ý chính toàn bài (R4Q1) và Thái độ tác giả (R4Q10).

tasks.title:
You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. A young man named Tom recently applied for a job at your restaurant and sent you an email asking for more details.

Read part of his email below.
tasks.content:
Thank you for considering my application. Before I confirm, I'd like to ask a few questions about the position.

  • Which branch would I be working at?
  • What would my main responsibilities be?
  • What are the benefits of this job, and what is the salary?
tasks.description: Respond to Tom's email and answer all of his questions. You should write at least 120 words. You don't need to include your name or addresses. Your response will be evaluated in terms of Task Fulfillment, Organization, Vocabulary and Grammar.
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài và xác định dạng đề:

Đây là dạng Email trả lời (Formal) cho một người đã ứng tuyển vào nhà hàng của bạn. Bạn cần trả lời đầy đủ 3 câu hỏi chính: làm việc ở chi nhánh nào, trách nhiệm công việc là gì, và lợi ích cùng mức lương của công việc. Yêu cầu tối thiểu 120 từ, giọng văn thân thiện, cởi mở nhưng vẫn cung cấp thông tin rõ ràng, cụ thể để ứng viên nắm được công việc.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục logic (Organization):

  • Greeting: Chào hỏi. Ví dụ: Dear Tom,
  • Opening: Cảm ơn và dẫn vào chủ đề. Ví dụ: Thank you for your interest in joining our team. I'm happy to answer your questions.
  • Body 1 (Branch): Nêu chi nhánh làm việc. Ví dụ: You would be working at our branch on Nguyen Hue Street, which is our busiest and most popular location.
  • Body 2 (Responsibilities): Nêu trách nhiệm công việc. Ví dụ: Your main responsibilities would include taking orders, serving customers, and helping to keep the dining area clean and organized.
  • Body 3 (Benefits & Salary): Nêu lợi ích và lương. Ví dụ: As for benefits, you'll receive free meals during shifts and health insurance after three months, with a starting salary of 6 million VND per month.
  • Closing: Kết thúc thư và mời phản hồi thêm. Ví dụ: Please let me know if you have any further questions.
  • Sign-off: Best regards, [Your Name].

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Vocabulary & Grammar):

Sử dụng thì Hiện tại đơn để mô tả công việc và các cấu trúc liệt kê (include, such as) khi nêu trách nhiệm. Đưa ra số liệu cụ thể (lương, thời gian) để câu trả lời thuyết phục hơn.

Từ vựng quan trọng:

  • Job responsibilities: Trách nhiệm công việc
  • Starting salary: Mức lương khởi điểm
  • Health insurance: Bảo hiểm y tế
  • Working hours: Giờ làm việc
  • Staff benefits: Phúc lợi nhân viên
  • Branch location: Vị trí chi nhánh
  • Probation period: Thời gian thử việc

Từ nối (Linking words):

  • First of all: Trước hết
  • In terms of: Về mặt
  • Additionally: Thêm vào đó
  • As for: Còn về
  • Lastly: Cuối cùng

Cách diễn đạt cảm xúc (Expressing feelings):

  • I'm happy to answer...: Tôi rất vui được trả lời...
  • We'd love to have you...: Chúng tôi rất mong được có bạn...
  • Feel free to ask...: Đừng ngại hỏi thêm...

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Chỉ trả lời 1-2 trong số 3 câu hỏi mà đề bài yêu cầu.
  • Đưa ra thông tin quá chung chung, không có số liệu hay chi tiết cụ thể.
  • Dùng văn phong quá thân mật như viết cho bạn bè trong khi đây là ngữ cảnh công việc.

5. Cách kiểm tra bài trong 2 phút cuối:

  • Đếm lại số từ, đảm bảo đạt tối thiểu 120 từ.
  • Kiểm tra đã trả lời đủ cả 3 câu hỏi (chi nhánh, trách nhiệm, lợi ích/lương) chưa.
  • Rà soát lại các con số và thông tin đã nêu có nhất quán không.

6. Tư duy làm bài:

Hãy tưởng tượng bạn đang thật sự tuyển dụng và muốn cung cấp thông tin rõ ràng, chuyên nghiệp nhưng vẫn thân thiện để ứng viên cảm thấy được chào đón.

tasks.title: You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.
tasks.content:
Nowadays, it is common to see people buying clothes and other products that are similar to those owned by their friends.

Some people believe that this helps them feel more connected to their friends and fit in with their social circle, while others think that everyone should express their own individual style regardless of what their friends choose.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
tasks.description: Write an essay to an educated reader to discuss both views and give your own opinion about people buying clothes and other products similar to their friends. Include reasons and any relevant examples to support your answer. You should write at least 250 words. Your response will be evaluated in terms of Task Fulfilment, Organization, Vocabulary and Grammar.
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài và xác định dạng bài:

Đây là dạng bài Discussion Essay, bàn về việc nhiều người mua quần áo và các sản phẩm giống với bạn bè của mình. Bạn cần trình bày cả hai quan điểm: một bên cho rằng điều này giúp gắn kết với bạn bè, bên còn lại cho rằng mỗi người nên có phong cách riêng. Yêu cầu tối thiểu 250 từ, tránh chỉ tập trung vào một phía.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục (Organization):

  • Introduction: Giới thiệu hiện tượng và nêu hai luồng quan điểm. Ví dụ: It has become increasingly common for people to purchase items similar to those of their friends, and opinions on this trend vary widely.
  • Body 1 (Quan điểm 1): Topic sentence → Explanation → Example. Ví dụ: On the one hand, some people believe that owning similar items helps them feel more connected to their friends and strengthens their sense of belonging.
  • Body 2 (Quan điểm 2): Ví dụ: On the other hand, others argue that everyone should express their own individuality rather than simply following what their friends buy.
  • Body 3 (Ý kiến cá nhân): Ví dụ: In my opinion, while it is natural to be influenced by friends, personal choices should ultimately reflect one's own tastes and needs.
  • Conclusion: Khẳng định lại quan điểm. Ví dụ: In conclusion, both social connection and personal identity matter, but individuality should not be sacrificed entirely for the sake of fitting in.

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Vocabulary & Grammar):

Sử dụng thì Hiện tại đơn để nêu sự thật và quan điểm chung, kết hợp cấu trúc nhượng bộ (although, while) để liên kết hai luồng ý kiến mạch lạc hơn. Có câu Thesis Statement rõ ràng ở phần mở bài.

Từ vựng quan trọng:

  • Peer influence: Ảnh hưởng từ bạn bè
  • Sense of belonging: Cảm giác thuộc về một nhóm
  • Personal identity: Bản sắc cá nhân
  • Social circle: Nhóm bạn xã hội
  • Consumer behavior: Hành vi tiêu dùng
  • Individuality: Cá tính riêng
  • Conform to a trend: Tuân theo xu hướng

Từ nối (Linking words):

  • On the one hand / On the other hand: Một mặt / Mặt khác (Thêm ý)
  • However / Nevertheless: Tuy nhiên (Đối lập)
  • As a result: Do đó (Nguyên nhân - kết quả)
  • For example / For instance: Ví dụ như (Minh họa)
  • In conclusion / To sum up: Tóm lại (Kết luận)
  • Similarly / Likewise: Tương tự (Thêm ý tương đồng)

Diễn đạt lại ý (Paraphrasing):

  • Purchasing similar items: Thay cho "buying the same things".
  • Following friends' choices: Thay cho "copying friends".
  • Personal self-expression: Thay cho "individual style".

Cách diễn đạt ý kiến / so sánh:

  • From my perspective...: Theo quan điểm của tôi...
  • Unlike those who prefer...: Không giống những người thích...
  • A more balanced approach would be...: Một cách tiếp cận cân bằng hơn sẽ là...

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Chỉ trình bày một quan điểm mà bỏ qua quan điểm còn lại.
  • Không có Topic sentence rõ ràng ở mỗi đoạn thân bài.
  • Lạm dụng ví dụ chung chung, thiếu tính thuyết phục.

5. Cách kiểm tra bài trong 3–5 phút cuối:

  • Kiểm tra xem đã có Thesis Statement rõ ràng ở mở bài chưa.
  • Đảm bảo cả hai quan điểm đều được thảo luận đầy đủ.
  • Rà soát lỗi ngữ pháp và sự liên kết giữa các đoạn.

6. Tư duy làm bài:

Đừng vội nghiêng về một phía ngay từ đầu. Hãy phân tích khách quan cả hai luồng ý kiến, sau đó mới đưa ra quan điểm cá nhân dựa trên lập luận vững chắc.

questions: How often do you check your email?
What do you usually use email for?
Do you think email is still an important way of communication nowadays?
What type of physical activity do you enjoy the most?
How do you usually make time for exercise in your daily schedule?
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài:

  • Phần thi này kéo dài 3 phút với 6 câu hỏi, được giám khảo hỏi trực tiếp theo hình thức hội thoại tự nhiên.
  • Chủ đề A (Email): Ba câu hỏi đầu xoay quanh tần suất kiểm tra email, mục đích sử dụng và tầm quan trọng của email trong giao tiếp hiện đại.
  • Chủ đề B (Tập thể dục): Ba câu hỏi sau khai thác thói quen tập luyện, môn thể thao yêu thích và cách sắp xếp thời gian cho việc rèn luyện sức khỏe.
  • Tiêu chí chấm điểm gồm: Độ trôi chảy (Fluency), Từ vựng (Vocabulary), Ngữ pháp (Grammar) và Phát âm (Pronunciation).
  • Nên phân bổ khoảng 25–30 giây cho mỗi câu hỏi, tránh dồn quá nhiều thời gian cho một chủ đề.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):

  • Áp dụng cấu trúc Answer – Reason – Example (ARE): trả lời trực tiếp, đưa lý do, sau đó minh họa bằng ví dụ cụ thể.
  • Ví dụ Chủ đề A: "I check my email several times a day, mainly to keep up with work-related messages and university announcements."
  • Ví dụ Chủ đề B: "Yes, I try to exercise at least three times a week, usually by jogging in the morning before classes start."
  • Luôn tự hỏi Why?/How? sau mỗi câu trả lời ngắn để mở rộng ý (bắt buộc).
  • Dùng một câu chuyển ý ngắn gọn khi chuyển từ Chủ đề A sang B, ví dụ: "Now, shifting to a different aspect of my daily routine..." (bắt buộc).

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):

  • Giữ tốc độ nói đều, sử dụng các từ đệm tự nhiên như "well", "actually" để tránh im lặng kéo dài.
  • Về thì: dùng hiện tại đơn khi nói về thói quen sử dụng email và tập luyện ("I usually...", "I tend to..."), dùng hiện tại hoàn thành nếu nhắc đến trải nghiệm tích lũy ("I have used email for work since I started my job").
  • Nếu quên từ, hãy diễn giải bằng cách mô tả (paraphrase) thay vì dừng lại.
  • Từ vựng Chủ đề A: inbox (hộp thư đến), attachment (tệp đính kèm), formal correspondence (thư từ trang trọng), stay in touch (giữ liên lạc).
  • Từ vựng Chủ đề B: work out (tập luyện), stay in shape (giữ dáng), burn calories (đốt calo), squeeze in some time (sắp xếp thời gian).

Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:

  • a quick and convenient way to communicate (cách giao tiếp nhanh và tiện lợi) — Chủ đề A.
  • respond to emails promptly (phản hồi email kịp thời) — Chủ đề A.
  • an official channel of communication (kênh giao tiếp chính thức) — Chủ đề A.
  • maintain a healthy lifestyle (duy trì lối sống lành mạnh) — Chủ đề B.
  • relieve stress (giải tỏa căng thẳng) — Chủ đề B.
  • fit exercise into a busy schedule (sắp xếp việc tập luyện vào lịch trình bận rộn) — Chủ đề B.

Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):

  • Actually, – mở đầu ý kiến cá nhân tự nhiên (thực ra thì).
  • In terms of... – giới hạn phạm vi câu trả lời (về mặt...).
  • Apart from that, – bổ sung ý (bên cạnh đó).
  • The main reason is that... – nêu lý do chính.
  • Speaking of... – chuyển chủ đề mượt mà (nói đến...).

Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:

  • "Personally, I think email is still essential, especially for formal or professional matters." (Cá nhân tôi nghĩ...) — Chủ đề A.
  • "From my point of view, quick messaging apps have replaced email for casual conversations." (Theo quan điểm của tôi...) — Chủ đề A.
  • "As far as I'm concerned, regular exercise is key to both physical and mental well-being." (Theo tôi thì...) — Chủ đề B.

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Trả lời cụt lủn kiểu "Yes" hoặc "Every day" mà không giải thích thêm — đây là lỗi nghiêm trọng nhất.
  • Với Chủ đề A: nhầm lẫn giữa "email" (danh từ) và "e-mail somebody" (động từ), hoặc phát âm sai từ "attachment".
  • Với Chủ đề B: chỉ nói "I like sports" chung chung mà không nêu cụ thể môn thể thao nào.
  • Dùng sai thì, ví dụ dùng thì tương lai khi mô tả thói quen hiện tại.

5. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:

  • Dùng câu chêm: "That's an interesting question, let me think for a moment" để có thêm thời gian.
  • Nếu quên từ vựng cụ thể, hãy mô tả bằng từ đơn giản hơn, ví dụ thay vì "cardio" có thể nói "exercise that makes your heart beat faster".
  • Với Chủ đề A, nếu không nhớ chi tiết, có thể nói chung chung về "checking emails for work and study" rồi phát triển thêm.
  • Với Chủ đề B, nếu bí ý tưởng, hãy liên hệ đến lợi ích sức khỏe của việc tập luyện để kéo dài câu trả lời.

6. Tư duy làm bài nói:

  • Hãy xem đây như một cuộc trò chuyện thân mật, không phải một bài kiểm tra căng thẳng.
  • Khi chuyển từ Chủ đề A sang B, hãy "reset" tâm lý và coi đó là một câu hỏi hoàn toàn mới.
  • Ưu tiên sự tự nhiên và trôi chảy hơn là cố gắng dùng từ vựng học thuật phức tạp.

tasks.situation:
Your company is planning an annual company trip for all employees.

You are considering the following options:

  • Option 1: A trip to a riverside area
  • Option 2: A trip to a theme park
  • Option 3: A camping trip in the countryside

Choose the best option and explain your reasons.
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài:

  • Tình huống: công ty của bạn đang lên kế hoạch tổ chức chuyến đi chơi thường niên cho toàn bộ nhân viên.
  • Ba lựa chọn: đi ven sông (riverside), công viên giải trí (theme park), và cắm trại ở vùng quê (camping).
  • Tiêu chí chấm điểm: khả năng phân tích, so sánh và đưa ra kết luận thuyết phục, cùng với Fluency, Vocabulary, Grammar và Pronunciation.
  • Thời gian: 4 phút — khoảng 1 phút chuẩn bị và 3 phút trình bày.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):

  • Sử dụng cấu trúc I-C-E (Introduction – Comparison/Body – End): giới thiệu tình huống, phân tích lần lượt ba lựa chọn, sau đó kết luận và đưa ra lý do.
  • Option 1 (riverside): "A riverside trip offers a peaceful setting for relaxation, but it may not provide enough activities to keep everyone engaged."
  • Option 2 (theme park): "A theme park is exciting and suitable for all age groups, though it can be quite costly and crowded during holidays."
  • Option 3 (camping): "Camping encourages teamwork and closer bonding among colleagues, but it might be physically demanding for those who are not used to outdoor conditions."
  • Mẹo: luôn neo lập luận vào bối cảnh thực tế của một chuyến đi tập thể công ty (bắt buộc).
  • Mẹo: dùng từ nối tương phản như "however", "on the other hand" để chuyển giữa ưu và nhược điểm (bắt buộc).

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):

  • Liên kết ba lựa chọn với nhau thay vì nói tách biệt, ví dụ: "Compared to Option 2, Option 3 promotes stronger team bonding."
  • Về thì: dùng câu điều kiện loại 1 khi dự đoán hệ quả ("If we go camping, we will need to prepare more carefully") và hiện tại đơn khi mô tả đặc điểm từng lựa chọn.
  • Paraphrase cụm "company trip" thành "team-building trip" hoặc "corporate outing" để tránh lặp từ.

Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:

  • team bonding (gắn kết đồng đội).
  • a relaxing getaway (chuyến đi thư giãn).
  • budget-friendly (tiết kiệm chi phí).
  • outdoor activities (hoạt động ngoài trời).
  • suitable for all ages (phù hợp với mọi lứa tuổi).
  • logistics arrangement (sắp xếp hậu cần).

Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):

  • On the other hand, – nêu quan điểm đối lập (mặt khác).
  • Compared to..., – so sánh giữa các lựa chọn.
  • Taking everything into account, – tổng kết trước khi kết luận (xét tổng thể).
  • Nevertheless, – nhấn mạnh điểm trái ngược (tuy nhiên).
  • As a result, – nêu hệ quả (kết quả là).

Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:

  • "If it were up to me, I would choose the camping trip because it strengthens teamwork the most." (Nếu là tôi...)
  • "I would strongly recommend the theme park for its fun and lively atmosphere." (Tôi sẽ khuyên...)
  • "In my opinion, a riverside trip offers the best balance between relaxation and cost." (Theo ý kiến của tôi...)

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Chỉ khen lựa chọn mình chọn mà không chỉ ra nhược điểm của các lựa chọn còn lại.
  • Lặp đi lặp lại từ "fun"/"good" thay vì dùng tính từ học thuật hơn như "engaging", "cost-effective".
  • Không đưa ra kết luận rõ ràng ở cuối bài nói.

5. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:

  • Nếu quên từ vựng chuyên ngành, chuyển hướng sang yếu tố chi phí hoặc sự thuận tiện để tiếp tục lập luận.
  • Dùng câu chêm: "Let's evaluate this option from a different perspective" để có thêm thời gian suy nghĩ.
  • Nếu bí ý ở một lựa chọn, hãy bình tĩnh chuyển sang phân tích lựa chọn tiếp theo.

6. Tư duy làm bài nói:

  • Hãy suy nghĩ như một nhân viên thực sự đang góp ý cho công ty — điều gì thực sự phù hợp với đa số mọi người.
  • Đưa ra một vài gợi ý cải thiện ngay cả cho lựa chọn được chọn để thể hiện tư duy phản biện.
  • Sự mạch lạc và logic trong lập luận quan trọng hơn việc dùng từ vựng phức tạp.

tasks.topic: The key factors that make a training workshop successful
followUp: What do you think makes a training workshop successful?
How can a company measure whether a workshop has achieved its goals?
If a company has a limited budget, what aspects of a workshop could be downsized without affecting its quality?
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài:

  • Chủ đề: Những yếu tố tạo nên một buổi training workshop thành công, với 3 nhánh ý chính và 1 nhánh ý cá nhân (gợi ý nhánh thứ 4: vai trò của phản hồi sau workshop).
  • Tiêu chí chấm điểm: khả năng phát triển ý mạch lạc theo sơ đồ tư duy, cùng Fluency, Vocabulary, Grammar và Pronunciation.
  • Thời gian: 5 phút; khoảng 3–3.5 phút cho bài nói chính, phần còn lại dành cho câu hỏi follow-up.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):

  • Sử dụng cấu trúc IDEA (Introduction – Detail – Example – Add/wrap up) vì chủ đề mang tính công việc/tổ chức, cần cả lý lẽ lẫn ví dụ thực tế.
  • Ví dụ 1 (mở bài): "A successful training workshop depends on several key factors, from careful planning to active participant engagement."
  • Ví dụ 2 (nhánh cá nhân): "Personally, I believe collecting feedback after the workshop is just as important as the workshop itself, as it helps organizers improve future sessions."
  • Mẹo: khi nói về từng nhánh ý, hãy đưa ra một ví dụ workshop cụ thể để minh họa thay vì chỉ nói lý thuyết.
  • Mẹo: bám sát sơ đồ tư duy để tránh lan man, không lặp lại ý đã nói (bắt buộc).

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):

  • Dùng cụm từ chuyển tiếp mượt mà giữa các nhánh ý, ví dụ "Another crucial factor is...".
  • Về thì: dùng hiện tại đơn để nêu sự thật/quan điểm chung ("A good trainer keeps participants engaged") và hiện tại hoàn thành để nói về trải nghiệm tích lũy ("I have attended several workshops on soft skills").
  • Paraphrase "training workshop" bằng "training session" hoặc "professional development program" để tránh lặp từ.

Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:

  • clear-cut objectives (mục tiêu rõ ràng).
  • hands-on activities (hoạt động thực hành).
  • keep participants engaged (giữ người tham gia hứng thú).
  • subject-matter expert (chuyên gia trong lĩnh vực).
  • practical takeaways (bài học thực tiễn mang về).
  • post-workshop feedback (phản hồi sau buổi workshop).

Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):

  • To begin with, – mở đầu nhánh ý đầu tiên (trước hết).
  • Moreover, – bổ sung ý (hơn nữa).
  • Another point worth noting is... – chuyển sang nhánh ý mới.
  • In addition to that, – mở rộng ý (thêm vào đó).
  • To sum up, – kết luận (tóm lại).

Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:

  • "I would say that a well-structured agenda is the backbone of any successful workshop." (Tôi cho rằng...)
  • "From what I've experienced, interactive sessions are far more memorable than lecture-style presentations." (Theo những gì tôi trải nghiệm được...)
  • "It seems to me that the trainer's ability to engage the audience matters just as much as the content itself." (Đối với tôi thì có vẻ như...)

4. Gợi ý trả lời câu hỏi follow-up:

  • "What do you think makes a training workshop successful?" – Clear objectives, an engaging trainer, and practical, interactive content that participants can apply afterward.
  • "How can a company measure whether a workshop has achieved its goals?" – Through participant feedback surveys, follow-up assessments, and observing whether new skills are applied at work.
  • "If a company has a limited budget, what aspects of a workshop could be downsized without affecting its quality?" – Elements like venue luxury, catering, or printed materials could be reduced, while keeping the trainer's quality and core content intact.

5. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Chỉ liệt kê ý mà không giải thích hoặc cho ví dụ cụ thể.
  • Quên nhánh ý cá nhân — nên chuẩn bị trước một quan điểm riêng liên quan đến workshop.
  • Dành quá nhiều thời gian cho bài nói chính, không còn thời gian trả lời follow-up.

6. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:

  • Neo vào một buổi workshop hoặc khóa đào tạo thực tế mà bản thân từng tham gia khi bí ý.
  • Câu chêm học thuật: "That is a complex issue. If we evaluate it from a societal viewpoint..."
  • Nếu quên từ vựng chuyên ngành, dùng mô tả đơn giản, ví dụ thay vì "facilitator" có thể nói "the person who leads and guides the workshop".

7. Tư duy làm bài nói:

  • Suy nghĩ từ góc nhìn của cả người tổ chức lẫn người tham gia workshop.
  • Sự mạch lạc và logic trong luồng ý là yếu tố then chốt để đạt điểm cao.
  • Đừng cố nhồi nhét từ vựng khó, hãy ưu tiên truyền tải ý tưởng rõ ràng và tự nhiên.
